absent: Participatory action research appears only through one 2021 review: there is no Fals Borda, Freire or Latin American PAR, nothing decolonial or Global South, and no complexity theory of the Juarrero, Levin or Tsing kind despite the paper's systems framing.
forYou: If you want this model for 'Substrate Matters' or the CDC Urban Innovation workshops, note that its ancestry is soft systems plus training evaluation, not participatory or decolonial research, so it will measure whether a workshop ran well rather than whether it shifted who holds the knowledge.
method: References read from the Springer article page rather than Crossref, which was blocked this run; strands and narrative by Claude, grounded only in the reference list and title. One entry ('REBUILD') carries no author or year on the page and is recorded as listed.
narrative:
The spine of this reference list is British soft systems thinking. Checkland's thirty-year retrospective (2000) sits at the root, and Jackson carries it forward twice over: first as creative holism and critical systems practice (2006), then in a 2025 reassessment that reads systems thinking through action research. Midgley's community operational research (2018), Herron (2025) and Weaver (2026) keep that line current, and Rosenhead's survey of problem structuring methods (2006) with Tavella's study of facilitated modelling (2015) supply the mechanics of getting a group to think together.

Grafted onto that root is a quite different literature: how to run a workshop. Gray's Gamestorming (2010), Storvang (2017) and Thoring (2020) treat the workshop as a research instrument, while Pavelin (2014), Sufi (2018) and Fadlelmola (2019) are 'ten simple rules' guidance. The evaluation half of the paper comes from somewhere else again: Kirkpatrick's four levels (2006, 2007), applied to research-methods training by Abdulghani (2014) and set against Rushmer's realist evaluation of knowledge exchange (2014).

Participation enters late and thinly. Scharmer's Theory U (2015), Ellstrom's interactive research (2020) and Keahey's review of participatory action research and sustainable development (2021) are the only places where the question of whose knowledge counts is put directly, and none of them is load-bearing. The median year is 2017, so this is a recent list, but its newest sources (Stapleton 2026, Pathan 2023) are the Irish circular-economy case rather than the methodology.
